extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, students of mathematics, and general readers interested in the philosophy/values of mathematical work
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the value and justification of mathematical work and a mathematician's life—contrasting practical utility, aesthetic/creative value, mentorship, and ethical consequences of applicability. Extracted from G. H. Hardy's A Mathematician's Apology (selections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical utility (elementary mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is undeniable that a good deal of elementary mathematics... has considerable practical utility."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy defines 'elementary' as what professional mathematicians include (e.g., a fair working knowledge of differential and integral calculus). He notes these parts are on the whole dull and have the least aesthetic value — useful but aesthetically inferior to higher mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic value of 'real' mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: "The 'real' mathematics of the 'real' mathematicians, the mathematics of Fermat and Euler and Gauss and Abel and Riemann, is almost wholly 'useless' (and this is as true of 'applied' as of 'pure' mathematics)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy asserts that the deepest, most admired mathematics is largely without practical application; its lack of utility does not diminish its aesthetic worth. This distinguishes 'real' mathematics from merely useful elementary parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics cannot be justified solely by utility
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is not possible to justify the life of any genuine professional mathematician on the ground of the 'utility' of his work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The attempt to defend mathematical practice purely by appeal to practical benefit is rejected. Practical standards may rate mathematical lives as having nil value even when the mathematician believes otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uselessness can be a protective/ethical virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Hardy addresses the misconception that pure mathematicians 'glory in the uselessness' of their work and explains that the remoteness of mathematics can 'keep it gentle and clean.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He reasons that if number theory could be used for clearly honourable practical ends, mathematicians would welcome that; but because science can serve evil (particularly in war), remoteness/uselessness may be a reason for rejoicing since it reduces the chance of misuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution as creation: adding to knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have added something to knowledge, and helped others to add more; and that these somethings have a value..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy offers creation (adding to knowledge) as the primary justification of a mathematician's life: producing new mathematics is analogous to creating works of art and can be judged for its intrinsic value rather than its utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and mentorship as part of a mathematician's value
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have helped to train other mathematicians... and their work has been, so far at any rate as I have helped them to it, as useless as my own."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching and mentoring other mathematicians is presented as a component of one’s mathematical life and contribution; it extends influence but may still be judged 'useless' by external practical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical creations judged like artistic creations
rubrics_metrics.description: "these somethings have a value which differs in degree only, and not in kind, from that of the creations of the great mathematicians, or of any of the other artists..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hardy argues that the value of mathematical work should be assessed on aesthetic/creative grounds comparable to those used for art: mathematical works are creations whose worth is of the same kind as artistic creations, differing only in degree.
